source_lines_after.36: [A1] Relative boundedness supplies finite $a,b\ge0$ with $a<1$ and $\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ on $D(A)$. The graph norm is $(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$; graph closure defines the operator closure. source_lines_after.38: [A2] Symmetry is the identity $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ on the domain; self-adjoint operators are closed and densely defined. A densely defined symmetric $S$ is self-adjoint if both ranges of $S\pm i\mu$ equal $H$ for some $\mu>0$. Nonreal points are resolvent points of a self-adjoint operator. The convention is $R_T(z)=(z-T)^{-1}$. [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]] [[thm-self-adjointness-range-criterion]] [[thm-self-adjoint-resolvent-estimate]] [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]
source_lines_after.40: [A3] If a bounded operator $C$ has norm less than one, $I-C$ has a bounded inverse given by the Neumann series. [[lem-neumann-series]]
source_lines_after.42: [A4] On a nonzero $H$, a self-adjoint $T$ has a regular PVM $E$, domain $\{x:\int v^2dE_x<\infty\}$, and $\|T x\|^2=\int v^2dE_x$, $\langle Tx,x\rangle=\int v\,dE_x$. Bounded integrals satisfy the norm bound and quadratic identity. Projections multiply by intersection; strong countable additivity holds. The Borel calculus has the product rule with domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$, and the spectrum of $T$ is the set of $v$ for which every neighborhood has nonzero projection (apply its essential-range assertion to $f(v)=v$). [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] [[lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed]] [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]] [[def-projection-valued-measure]] [[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]

source_lines_after.52: 1.1 If $H=\{0\}$, all domains and graphs are zero and all conclusions hold directly. Otherwise use [A4]. For $z=\pm i\mu$, $\mu>0$, put $r_z(v)=(z-v)^{-1}$. The bounds $|r_z(v)|\le1/\mu$ and $|v r_z(v)|\le1$ show that $r_z(A)$ maps $H$ into $D(A)$, that $\|r_z(A)\|\le1/\mu$, and that $\|A r_z(A)\|\le1$. The product rule gives $(z-A)r_z(A)=I$ on $H$ and $r_z(A)(z-A)=I$ on $D(A)$, so this is $R_A(z)$. Thus $\|BR_A(z)\|\le a+b/\mu<1$ when, for example, $\mu=1+2b/(1-a)$. [A1, A2, A4, given]
source_lines_after.54: 1.2 For any nonzero-space self-adjoint $T$ and real $c$, the spectral-measure equivalence $T\ge c$ if and only if $E(( -\infty,c))=0$ follows directly. If $T\ge c$ and $J_n=[-(n+1),c-1/(n+1)]$ has a nonzero projection, a nonzero $x$ in its range belongs to $D(T)$, has $E_x$ carried by $J_n$, and satisfies $\langle Tx,x\rangle\le(c-1/(n+1))\|x\|^2$, a contradiction. These increasing sets exhaust $(-\infty,c)$, so countable additivity gives zero projection. Conversely zero projection below $c$ gives $\langle Tx,x\rangle=\int v\,dE_x\ge c\|x\|^2$ for every $x$ in $D(T)$. Also if every real $t<c$ is a resolvent point, the essential-range characterization in [A4] supplies a zero-projection open neighborhood of each $t$. The rational intervals contained in such neighborhoods form a countable cover of $(-\infty,c)$; their union has zero projection by countable subadditivity of each $E_x$. Therefore again $T\ge c$. This does not require a finite spectral infimum or any resolvent-distance formula. [A4]
source_lines_after.56: 2.1 Put $S=A+B$ on exactly $D(A)$. For $z=\pm i\mu$ the identity $z-S=(I-BR_A(z))(z-A)$ holds on $D(A)$, since $R_A(z)(z-A)x=x$ there. The first factor is boundedly invertible by [A3], and $z-A$ is bijective $D(A)$ to $H$. Hence both nonreal shifts of $S$ are onto. $S$ is symmetric by summing the two symmetry identities and densely defined because $D(A)$ is dense. The range criterion makes $S$ self-adjoint. No second-resolvent identity with a previously closed $S$ is assumed. [A1, A2, A3, step 1.1]
source_lines_after.58: 3.1 Suppose $A\ge\gamma$ and let $\lambda+\gamma=d>0$. By step 1.2 $E_A$ is carried by $[\gamma,\infty)$. Define $r(v)=(-\lambda-v)^{-1}$ on that half-line and zero outside. For $v\ge\gamma$, $|r(v)|\le1/d$ and $|v r(v)|\le\max(1,|\gamma|/d)$: for $v\ge0$ the ratio $v/(v+\lambda)$ is monotone with its maximum at an endpoint or its limiting value $1$; for $\gamma\le v<0$, $(-v)/(v+\lambda)$ decreases with $v$ since $\lambda>0$ in that case. The spectral product rule shows $r(A)=R_A(-\lambda)$, exactly as in step 1.1, and hence $\|BR_A(-\lambda)\|\le a\max(1,|\gamma|/d)+b/d$. Put $C=\max\{a|\gamma|+b,b/(1-a)\}$. For every $d>C$ this last bound is strictly below one: if $d\ge|\gamma|$ it equals $a+b/d<1$ (also when $b=0$); if $d<|\gamma|$ it equals $(a|\gamma|+b)/d<1$. The factorization of step 2.1 therefore proves that every real number $t<\gamma-C$ is in $\rho(S)$, with bounded inverse $R_A(t)(I-BR_A(t))^{-1}$. Apply step 1.2 to the already self-adjoint $S$ to obtain $S\ge\gamma-C$, the stated bound including its endpoint. [A1, A3, A4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2]
source_lines_after.60: 4.1 If $A$ is essentially self-adjoint, put $T=\overline A$. For each $x$ in $D(T)$ choose $x_n$ in $D(A)$ with $x_n\to x$ and $Ax_n\to Tx$, using [A5]. The inequality in [A1] applied to $x_n-x_m$ makes $Bx_n$ Cauchy. Define $\widetilde Bx$ as its limit. Two such approximations give the same limit by the same inequality applied to their difference. Approximating $x$ and $y$ and their linear combinations proves linearity, $\|\widetilde Bx\|\le a\|Tx\|+b\|x\|$, and symmetry by passing to the limit in $\langle Bx_n,y_n\rangle=\langle x_n,By_n\rangle$. It extends $B$ restricted to $D(A)$; no extension of $B$'s possibly larger domain is claimed. Step 2.1 makes $T+\widetilde B$ self-adjoint. The inclusion $A+B\subseteq T+\widetilde B$ and closedness give $\overline{A+B}\subseteq T+\widetilde B$. Conversely the same approximating sequences satisfy $(A+B)x_n\to(T+\widetilde B)x$, giving the reverse graph inclusion. This proves essential self-adjointness and the exact closure formula. If $A\ge\gamma$ in this case, taking limits of its quadratic inequality gives $T\ge\gamma$; step 3.1 then gives the bound for the closure and its restriction $A+B$. [A1, A2, A5, step 2.1, step 3.1]
